item.title: How a group that cannot communicate knows itself by its enemy
item.description: arXiv:2610.40835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Teams that cannot communicate seem stuck with what each member sees. We show that their opponent can tell them the rest. Silent hunters, jammed robots and traders who never meet all face an adversary that reacts to the group as a whole; every member can read that reaction, a tell, and learn what no member knows alone. One tell can do the work of a message from every member. The adversary would rather hide, but hiding interferes with its own task, and a team that commits in advance to how it will respond decides how much hiding is worth. A committed team never loses when its opponent cares more about its own goals, and does as well as a fully informed team exactly when the opponent's stake outweighs any gain from lying. Below that point the team learns more by trusting less: in a solved Gaussian model it obtains the truth by promising not to use all of it and keeps the cost the opponent would have paid to conceal; an exact test decides when this holds in finite games. How a team spreads its trust matters too. A lone uninformed member with a full-support prior needs a private coin, but with additive squared-error losses two interchangeable members who respond differently replace it, and a small discount on trust insures against misjudging the enemy. Information, on this view, is not only gathered or aggregated; it is produced by how a team commits to respond.
item.dc:creator: Gregory Falco

item.title: Renegotiable Options Fail to Prevent Hold-Up Between Two Profit-Maximizing Frontier LLM Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.40961v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Do contract terms that protect investment between people also protect it between profit-maximizing language-model agents? In the hold-up problem, a seller can adapt a unit to one buyer at a cost before the price is set. Once that cost is sunk, the buyer can offer almost nothing and the seller will still accept, so a seller who foresees this does not adapt. One remedy is an option: the buyer may buy at a fixed price. In theory the option stops working if the buyer can let it lapse and offer its own price instead. Yet in a laboratory experiment by Hoppe and Schmitz, this renegotiable option raised human investment from 41.5% of pairs without a contract to 67.2%. We had Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, each told to maximize its side's profit, play a one-shot game with the same strategic structure under their four contract regimes and a reference-price control. The agents did what game theory predicts: under the renegotiable option no seller adapted, and under the option that rules out this renegotiation every seller did. In a second experiment in which sellers no longer stated their expected revenue before deciding, removing the profit instruction left investment unchanged under no contract and both options. When we changed the numbers so that the buyer would exercise the option even without adaptation, adapting only added cost, and no seller adapted: the agents did not simply adapt whenever an option was offered or whenever its price covered the cost. Under our protocol, a contract term that raised investment between people did not protect it between agents.
item.dc:creator: Junwei Yao, Zike Yang, Yongxi Zhou, Yanxian Chen, Jianan Liu, Jiaxi Wen, Zhijun Wang

item.title: Kidney Exchange with Dual Donors
item.description: arXiv:2610.41466v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kidney exchange programs enable patients with incompatible living donors to receive transplants by exchanging donors with other patient-donor pairs. Existing models typically assume either that each patient enrolls with a single donor, or that at most one of a patient's multiple alternative donors is selected to donate. In practice, however, a patient may have access to multiple willing but incompatible donors who are all prepared to donate simultaneously if doing so enables the patient to receive a kidney. We study a dual-donor kidney exchange model, in which a patient may enroll with up to two proxy donors and the exchange is allowed to utilize both, provided the patient receives a compatible transplant. This paradigm allows a patient to participate in an exchange cycle via one donor while their second donor initiates a donation chain---unlocking additional transplants without relying on altruistic donors. We formulate the resulting combinatorial optimization problems under realistic cycle and chain constraints, showing that utilizing both donors introduces sharp computational challenges compared to standard exchange, and we design new approximation algorithms with provable guarantees. We also study strategic manipulation when patients hide a donor, establishing the limits of deterministic mechanisms and showing how randomization achieves truthfulness with near-optimal welfare. Finally, our experiments on realistic synthetic graphs demonstrate that using both donors yields substantial gains in total transplants over selecting at most one---even when only a small fraction of patients enroll with two donors.
item.dc:creator: Ioannis Caragiannis, Tomasz Filip Gawron, Kristoffer Arnsfelt Hansen, Yuchen Zhang

item.title: When Is a Game a Markov Decision Process? Correspondences Between Game Theory and Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.41962v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning and game theory describe the same object from two sides. Game theory says what a rational outcome of a strategic interaction is; reinforcement learning says how an agent could reach one through experience. The two literatures nevertheless keep separate vocabularies for identical structures, and the treatments that bridge them present the correspondence as analogy rather than theorem. This monograph supplies the theorems. A game is a Markov decision process in three distinct senses, and every table entry is labelled with the one that applies: a definitional identity, an exact reduction carried by a value- and solution-preserving map, or a structural analogy that fails under identifiable conditions. We take every standard class of game, from normal-form through repeated, stochastic, partially observable, extensive-form with imperfect information, Bayesian, graphical, Stackelberg, potential, coalitional, mean-field and evolutionary games, and identify for each the decision-theoretic model that reinforcement learning already studies under another name. The same treatment is applied to solution concepts: Nash equilibrium and the fixed point of the Bellman optimality operator, quantal response equilibrium and the soft Bellman operator, the Shapley value and credit assignment, Blackwell approachability and no-regret learning. We map each model class onto the training procedures sound for it and record the complexity of the associated solution problems. A final part collects the correspondences that do not hold: the non-stationarity that invalidates the independent-learner reduction, the impossibility results that forbid uncoupled convergence to Nash equilibrium, and the gap between the coarse correlated equilibria that no-regret self-play reaches and the correlated equilibria it is credited with.
item.dc:creator: Eduardo C. Garrido-Merch\'an

item.title: From Scalar Games to Unconstrained Network Zero-Sum Games: Transfer Principles for Gradient-Based Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.42087v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that, for a broad class of gradient-based learning rules, scalar zero-sum games form a complete test family for convergence in unconstrained network zero-sum games. Specifically, suppose a learning rule achieves last-iterate or time-average convergence on every scalar game of magnitude $a$ whenever $\eta\leq f(a)$, where $f$ is nonincreasing. Then the same guarantee holds on an arbitrary network zero-sum game with stacked game operator $\mathbf{G}$ whenever $\eta\leq f(\lVert\mathbf{G}\rVert_2)$. More generally, finite-time rate guarantees transfer mode by mode: the network response is bounded by the largest response of its scalar canonical games, and under compatible linear initialization conventions the worst-case finite-time network response is exactly the largest scalar canonical rate. Thus, understanding the learning dynamics on scalar games is sufficient to characterize universal convergence and worst-case rates over the corresponding class of network games. The result follows from the classical planar decomposition of real skew-symmetric game operators. Related mode-wise reasoning has appeared implicitly in spectral analyses of particular learning algorithms and in prior work using these decompositions for game representation and visualization; here we isolate the resulting transfer principle for gradient-based learning. We discuss implications for simplifying convergence analysis, time-average guarantees, low-dimensional geometric arguments, accelerated-method design, and worst-case numerical testing.
item.dc:creator: Gaoqi Xue, James P. Bailey

item.title: Strategic Tanking in Stable Matching Markets
item.description: arXiv:2610.42105v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motivated by a broad literature in psychology, organizational behavior, and matching markets, we introduce strategic tanking: an agent deliberately makes themselves less attractive to selected potential partners in order to improve their eventual assignment. Unlike traditional manipulation in stable matching, a tanker does not misreport whom they prefer; instead, they influence how others rank them. We show that tanking has a striking connection to classical preference manipulation. Cutoff tanking, in which an agent tanks with every potential partner below a chosen threshold, has exactly the same effect on the stable set as truncating one's own preference list at that threshold. Thus an agent can reproduce the power of a classical truncation while leaving their own preferences unchanged and every match acceptable. Arbitrary tanking, however, can go substantially further: under proposer-deferred acceptance, tanking equilibria can lie outside the sincere stable set. More broadly, whenever the sincere stable set contains multiple matchings, profitable strategic behavior remains available through either traditional preference manipulation or tanking, even when one side is restricted to honestly reporting their own preferences.
item.dc:creator: James P. Bailey

item.title: Fair Recommender Systems for Intersecting Groups
item.description: arXiv:2610.40936v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recommendation systems that optimize for the average user can fail to capture the preferences of diverse demographic groups. We consider a dynamic recommendation system, where arriving users can belong to different demographic groups. Importantly, these groups can intersect, and a user may belong to several groups. We first show that over time, any group-blind policy (which excludes all current-user group information) recommending $K \geq 1$ items incurs linear total regret under mild conditions. In turn, we introduce three group-aware algorithms based on the classical Upper Confidence Bound algorithm (UCB): i) Intersection-Fitting, which runs UCB on each intersection, but has a sublinear group- and intersection-level regret guarantee with an exponential dependence in the number of groups; and ii) two group-level heuristics, Inner-Outer UCB and Group-Item UCB which allocate different arms to different groups, and use a sleeping expert meta-learner to choose which active group's recommendation an intersection should inherit at any given time step. We provide experimental results on two datasets, Goodreads and BoardGameGeek, and highlight that our heuristics can be preferable to the intersection-fitting algorithm when intersection-level preferences are closely related to group-level preferences, but that intersection-fitting performs better when different intersections within a same group prefer different items.
item.dc:creator: Christine Ling, Juba Ziani

item.title: The Competitive Ratio of Online Budgeted Allocation is Strictly Smaller than $1-1/e$
item.description: arXiv:2610.41136v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A well-known conjecture in online algorithms is that the (randomized) competitive ratio of online budgeted allocation is $1-1/e$. We refute this conjecture and show that every randomized online algorithm has competitive ratio at most $1 - 1/e - \varepsilon$ for a (small) absolute constant $\varepsilon > 0$.
item.dc:creator: Debmalya Panigrahi, Ian Zhang

item.title: Truthful and Admissible Principal--Agent Testing with Nuisance Parameters
item.description: arXiv:2610.41283v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Statistical contracts reward experimenters according to the evidence produced by a costly study, so the reward rule influences both who participates and what they report. Principal--agent testing theory explains how to prevent ineffective proposals from being profitable. We ask when such contracts can also elicit honest parameter reports if the decision concerns a mean effect but the variance or distributional shape is unknown. Under risk neutrality and a fixed participation cost, we construct menus of e-values --- nonnegative normalized rewards with expected value at most one under every null --- such that (i) agents who know they are null have no incentive to participate, (ii) every alternative type earns positive expected profit and is thus incentivized to participate, (iii) truthful reporting uniquely maximizes expected their reward, (iv) and each contract is admissible: its payouts cannot be pointwise improved while retaining null validity. For Gaussian observations, we treat separately agents who know both mean and variance and agents who know only their mean; in the latter case, truthfulness holds at every variance without requiring a nuisance prior. Multi-sample extensions preserve these incentives and can reward accumulating evidence. Beyond Gaussian models, we show that two independent nonnegative observations suffice to elicit any finite mean above a positive null threshold, without any further distributional knowledge, but one observation cannot combine strict mean elicitation with individual admissibility on this class. Finally, we distinguish the existence of useful tests from the identification needed for truthful contracts. Boundedness is not required, and finitely many null constraints do not by themselves guarantee admissible elicitation.
item.dc:creator: Aaditya Ramdas

item.title: Branch-and-Cut for Mixed-Integer Nash Equilibrium Problems
item.description: arXiv:2506.02520v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider mixed-integer Nash equilibrium problems in which each player solves a mixed-integer optimization problem parameterized in the rivals' strategies. We distinguish standard Nash equilibrium problems (NEPs), where the parameterization acts only on the cost functions, and generalized NEPs (GNEPs), where the strategy spaces may also depend on the rivals' strategies. We introduce a branch-and-cut (B&C) algorithm for such games that, upon termination, either computes a pure Nash equilibrium or decides that none exists. The main idea is a bilevel reformulation based on the Nikaido--Isoda function. Using bilevel-optimization techniques, we obtain a tractable relaxation of this reformulation and embed it into a B&C framework. Depending on the setting, we derive sufficient conditions for the existence of suitable cuts and finite termination. For GNEPs, we adapt intersection cuts (ICs) from bilevel and mixed-integer linear optimization. Such cuts exist under assumptions that hold, e.g., for pure-integer GNEPs with decoupled concave objectives and linear coupling constraints. Since ICs may become arbitrarily shallow, we complement them with a fallback strategy that fixes recurring integer profiles and ensures finite termination in a relevant setting. For NEPs, suitable cuts always exist via best-response inequalities, and our method terminates finitely whenever the set of best-response sets is finite. This holds, e.g., if (i) the cost functions are concave in the players' own continuous strategies and the strategy sets are polyhedral, or (ii) the cost functions only depend on the player's own strategy and the rivals' integer strategy components. Numerical results on various NEPs and GNEPs show that our tailored B&C method outperforms directly applying the state-of-the-art bilevel solver MibS on the tested integer and generalized knapsack instances.
item.dc:creator: Alo\"is Duguet, Tobias Harks, Martin Schmidt, Julian Schwarz

item.title: Collusion-proof Auction Design using Side Information
item.description: arXiv:2511.12456v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bidder collusion degrades welfare and fairness in standard auctions. To address this, we introduce the Conditional-Posted Price (C-PoP) mechanism, a collusion-resilient design that uses machine learning classifiers to predict, even imprecisely, which bidders are colluding. C-PoP computes Posted Prices conditioned on predicted non-colluders' bids, ensuring truthfulness under perfect classification, thereby improving fairness toward non-colluders. Under imperfect classification, we bound overall and non-colluder welfare to establish the mechanism's robustness and fairness, respectively. Crucially, these bounds provide insights for classifier design, revealing that false negatives (misclassifying colluders as non-colluders) are preferable to false positives (misclassifying non-colluders as colluders). Numerical experiments show that C-PoP achieves strong performance in welfare, revenue, and fairness under collusion, even when using simple, low-cost classifiers.
item.dc:creator: Sukanya Kudva, Edward Dowling, Anil Aswani

item.title: Competing Auctions in Intermediated Markets
item.description: arXiv:2606.06633v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We analyze competing auctions in intermediated markets, where a seller selects among parallel mechanisms for the sale of a single good, most prominently the relay-and-protocol architecture of proposer-builder separation in Ethereum. When the intermediary can enforce single-homing on its bidders, sealed-bid second-price intermediary auctions fully unravel into the sealed first-price principal auction; open bidding-format intermediaries unravel only partially, collapsing into first-price in equilibrium under symmetric latency and sorting fast bidders to the intermediary under asymmetric latency. Any last-look advantage is removed through the availability of a credible sealed bidding channel. These results extend to multi-plexing environments (no enforcement by the intermediary). While the unraveling result indicates that the availability of a sealed first-price bidding channel pushes the overall market to the same auction structure, the very assumption of the credibility of such channel is problematic, as the seller may have an incentive to leak information: a first-price auction is leakage-resistant in the presence of a single ``fast'' bidder but not against two or more. However, if the seller can credibly commit to not leak bids, it is optimal for them to do so. A main motivation is the forthcoming Glamsterdam update of Ethereum: our analysis suggests that the availability of an in-protocol (first-price) bidding channel severely limits the design space for out-of-protocol auctions by relays and other intermediaries.
item.dc:creator: Bruno Mazorra, Minghao Pan, Christoph Schlegel

item.title: Simple Strategy-Iteration with Dantzig's Rule is not Strongly Polynomial on Turn-Based Deterministic Games
item.description: arXiv:2610.27386v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study turn-based deterministic zero-sum games with discounted and long-run average costs. For discounted costs, we establish exponential and superpolynomial iteration lower bounds for the simple strategy-iteration method with Dantzig's rule under unrestricted costs and unit weights, respectively. To the best of our knowledge, we establish for the first time that the method is not strongly polynomial, and this remains true even when all action costs belong to $\{-1,0,1\}$. For long-run average costs, we extend the Dantzig counterpart in~\cite{zhongye2026} to the two-player setting and prove that it terminates at an optimal strategy profile. However, a similar counterexample construction establishes an exponential iteration lower bound for termination with unrestricted costs. This construction does not extend to unit weights, for which we prove that the algorithm admits a strongly polynomial implementation.
item.dc:creator: Sanyou Mei

item.title: Index and Robustness of Mixed Equilibria: An Algebraic Approach
item.description: arXiv:2603.04298v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present two results regarding the relation of the index of equilibria and the index of fixed points, and the index of equilibria and payoff-robustness: any integer can be the index of an isolated completely mixed equilibrium of a finite game. In a particular class of isolated completely mixed equilibria, called monogenic, the index can be 0, +1 or -1 only. In this class non-zero index is equivalent to payoff-robustness. We also discuss extensions of the method of computation to extensive-form games, and cases where the equilibria might be located on the boundary of the strategy set. These results follow from a new method of computing indices of equilibria, which we also develop in this paper, that is based on algebraic properties of the system of polynomials describing completely mixed equilibria.
item.dc:creator: Lucas Pahl

item.title: GENSTRAT: Toward a Science of Strategic Reasoning in Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2605.23238v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Fixed game suites for evaluating strategic reasoning in large language models (LLMs) saturate and are hard to keep free of contamination. We introduce GENSTRAT, a system for evaluating the strategic capabilities of LLMs driven by procedural generation of two-player zero-sum imperfect-information betting games, allowing an evaluator to draw novel, fresh games on demand. Each game is characterized on a scale of five complexity axes (state space, temporal contingency, opponent dependence, private information, precision) and measured by Monte Carlo simulation. Using this generator, we construct a 50-game benchmark and hold a tournament of twelve frontier and open-weight models, gathering data from over 40,000 LLM vs. LLM matches. We further construct a composite complexity axis, and find that, on the eight hardest games, the gap between the best and worst model is 1.7x its value across the whole set of games. Ablations show that a higher thinking budget, disclosing the opponent's strategy, and higher reasoning matched to a game's specific demands (for private information and planning depth) were associated with higher margins for the LLM player.
item.dc:creator: Vartan Shadarevian, Kia Ghods, Alex Kenich, Anany Kotawala

item.title: Accelerating Min-Max Optimization via Power-Law Stepsizes
item.description: arXiv:2606.01764v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We revisit the convergence guarantees of the Extragradient (EG) method for unconstrained biaffine min-max optimization. It is known that EG with a fixed stepsize achieves a $\Theta(T^{-1/2})$ last-iterate convergence rate, which is slower than the optimal $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1})$ rate attainable by incorporating additional mechanisms such as anchoring. Motivated by recent advances showing that dynamic stepsizes alone can significantly accelerate gradient descent, we ask whether dynamic stepsizes can similarly accelerate the last-iterate convergence of EG. We present the first positive result in this direction. Specifically, we provide a deterministic dynamic stepsize schedule that accelerates the convergence rate of EG to $\mathcal{O}(T^{-2/3+\varepsilon})$ for any $\varepsilon > 0$. We also show that this rate is nearly tight when the extrapolation and update steps of EG use the same stepsize. We then show that allowing different stepsizes for the extrapolation and update steps further improves the convergence rate to the near-optimal $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1+\varepsilon})$. Our analysis reduces stepsize scheduling to an optimization problem, whose solution leads to a stepsize schedule that follows (a discretization of) a power-law distribution. Our proposed stepsize schedules and analysis extend to other methods, such as Optimistic Gradient (OG), and suggest broader applicability to general min-max optimization problems.
item.dc:creator: Yue Wu, Weiqiang Zheng, Yang Cai, Haipeng Luo
